docs.title: FieldNeuroToolbox (FNT)
docs.text:
Preprocessing and analysis toolbox for field and laboratory neurobehavioral data. FNT is open source and free for research and hobby use. It is released as-is and grows alongside our own research.

Bugs and feature requests: please open an issue.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text:
FNT bundles GUI tools for the common data types of field and laboratory neuroethology, in one desktop app that runs on an ordinary laptop:

  • Audio / USV

    Ultrasonic vocalization detection, classification and audio preprocessing, including the Classic Audio Detector (CAD).

  • Mask Audio Detector (MAD)

    Label calls on the spectrogram with SAM, train a segmentation model, and run it over thousands of recordings.

  • Video Processing

    Batch preprocessing, trimming, concatenation and manual behavioral scoring.

  • Video Tracking

    SAM-based interactive animal tracking for behavioral assays.

  • Mask Tracker

    Label animals with SAM, train a YOLO segmentation model, review its predictions and run it over whole videos.

  • UWB Tracking

    Ultra-wideband positions to cleaned, smoothed tracks, contact bouts, chases and region occupancy.

  • RFID Tracking

    Biomark reader downloads to cleaned reads, bouts, zone holders and co-occupancy, with QC reports.

  • Imaging

    Zeiss CZI microscopy viewing, processing and cell quantification.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The easiest way to use FNT is the pre-built standalone executable; no Python or Anaconda is needed.

  1. Download the latest release for your OS from the Releases page.
  2. Extract the archive.
  3. Run the fnt executable.

See Installation for the standalone requirements (ffmpeg) and for the development installation if you want to modify the code.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text: Video tutorials are posted to this YouTube playlist.

docs.title: Citing FNT
docs.text: If you use FNT in your research, please cite it. See Citing and license for the citation, the license and the attribution FNT's license asks of copies.

docs.title: Citing FNT
docs.text:
If you use FNT in published research, please cite it. The Cite this repository button on the GitHub page gives the citation in APA and BibTeX formats, generated from CITATION.cff:

@software{fnt,
  title  = {FieldNeuroToolbox (FNT)},
  author = {Vogt, Caleb C. and Garmany, Samuel and Lorman, Sophia G. and Donaldson, Zoe R.},
  url    = {https://github.com/calebvogt/fnt}
}

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: There are two ways to run FNT: the pre-built standalone executable (recommended for most users) or a development installation (if you want to modify the code).

docs.title: Standalone Executable (Recommended)
docs.text: You do not need to install Python or Anaconda for this version.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • ffmpeg — must be installed and on your system PATH for audio/video features. On Windows, see Installing ffmpeg on Windows below.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Download the latest release .zip or .tar.gz for your OS from the Releases page.
  2. Extract the archive.
  3. Run the extracted fnt executable to launch the GUI.

macOS security permission

Since the executable is unsigned, macOS Gatekeeper will block it. Open Terminal and run xattr -cr path/to/fnt on the extracted file (drag it from Finder into Terminal to paste the path). This removes the quarantine attribute from the executable and its bundled dependencies.

Windows SmartScreen

You may see a "Windows protected your PC" warning. Click More info → Run anyway.

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text: Use this method if you intend to modify the code or prefer managing your own Python environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Git on the command line (on your PATH). Installing GitHub Desktop alone is not sufficient — it bundles a git that isn't exposed to the terminal. The steps below install git into the conda environment.
  • Anaconda or Miniconda
  • Python 3.12 or newer (3.13 recommended; the codebase uses 3.12+ syntax)
  • ffmpeg — required for audio/video processing. Not a pip dependency, so pip install -e . alone does not provide it.

docs.title: Installing ffmpeg on Windows
docs.text:
Do not use conda install ffmpeg on Windows

The conda-forge ffmpeg package on Windows has a known DLL conflict (libintl / gdk-pixbuf / fontconfig) that causes it to crash during install and at runtime. Install ffmpeg system-wide instead.

  1. Download the "release essentials" zip from gyan.dev/ffmpeg/builds.
  2. Extract it to a permanent location, e.g. C:\ffmpeg.
  3. Add the bin folder (e.g. C:\ffmpeg\bin) to your system PATH: Settings → System → About → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables → Path → New.
  4. Open a new terminal and verify: ffmpeg -version.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/calebvogt/fnt.git
conda create --name fnt python=3.13
conda activate fnt
conda install git -y
cd path\to\fnt
pip install -e .

(ffmpeg is installed system-wide per the section above — do not conda install ffmpeg.)

docs.title: macOS / Linux
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/calebvogt/fnt.git
conda create --name fnt python=3.13
conda activate fnt
conda install git -y
conda install -c conda-forge ffmpeg -y
cd path/to/fnt
pip install -e .

On macOS/Linux the conda-forge ffmpeg package works fine.

docs.title: Launch the GUI
docs.text:
conda activate fnt
fnt

docs.title: GPU Support (Optional)
docs.text:
For SAM-based video tracking, the Mask Tracker and MAD training and inference, a GPU is a large speedup. Install PyTorch with CUDA support. The right command depends on your NVIDIA driver: MAD's Help ▸ Check GPU / CUDA setup… prints the exact pip command for your machine, or pick one on pytorch.org. For example, for CUDA 12.6:

conda activate fnt
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126

Verify GPU detection:

python -c "import torch; print('CUDA available:', torch.cuda.is_available())"

This requires an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support. Tools run on CPU otherwise, but significantly slower.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Because the package is installed in editable mode:

cd path/to/fnt
git pull

If the update changed pyproject.toml (new dependencies), re-run the install:

conda activate fnt
pip install -e .

docs.title: Exporting tables
docs.text:
File ▸ Export… writes folder-wide tables from the .mad files beside your recordings: one row per recording, one row per detection and one row per labelled call, all in one output folder. They are meant for analysis in R or pandas. mad export writes the same tables from the command line, with the same options.

This is different from File ▸ Export Annotations to CSV…, which writes one <recording>_FNT_MAD_annotations.csv beside each wav. Use that one to look at a single recording; use Export… to analyse a run.

docs.title: What it writes
docs.text:
File One row per Contents mad_recordings.csv recording whose last inference was the chosen model where it is, its start time and channel when the file name gives them, its duration, the model and when it ran, its detection and call counts mad_detections.csv detection of those recordings onset, score, review status, harmonic number, contour measures of its mask, brightness ridge mad_labelled_calls.csv labelled (accepted) call, from any model or painted by hand onset and offset, frequency box, MAD's call metrics recomputed from the audio, contour measures, brightness ridge, note and tags mad_call_images/<id>.png labelled call the call and 10 ms either side, every frequency bin (highest at the top); grey = level as MAD stores it, alpha = the call's own mask mad_export.json — how and when each table was last written (model, settings, inputs, FNT version)

The columns are generic. Anything particular to your experiment — trial, treatment, which animals were present, which zone a microphone covers — is not in the tables; join it in your analysis code, by folder, recording, channel or start.

Detections are the model's output: each row is the detection's mask as the model drew it, whatever its review status. Labelled calls are the reviewed masks, including edits and hand-painted calls.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Meaning Recordings The open project's recordings (the Audio list's with no project open), or folders, each searched to the bottom. Only recordings with a .mad file are exported; a recording whose wav has moved is still exported from its .mad. Output folder Where the tables go. Created if needed. Recordings and detections mad_recordings.csv and mad_detections.csv. No audio is read. Model Only recordings whose last inference was this model. The default is the model that analysed the most recordings; the list shows how many each model analysed. Labelled calls are not filtered by model. Labelled calls mad_labelled_calls.csv. Each labelled recording's audio is read to compute the call metrics, so this is the slow table. If the audio is missing the rows are written with those columns blank. Spectrogram images mad_call_images/, one PNG per labelled call. Implies Labelled calls. Include harmonics Off (the default): fundamentals only, i.e. calls whose harmonic_n is blank or 1. On: every detection and labelled call. Skip recordings unchanged since the last export On (the default): see below. Leave out .mad files written in the last N min Default 10. A .mad that changed this recently may still be open in MAD (an inference run in progress), so it is left out until the next export. A .mad that cannot be opened is left out the same way. Set 0 to include everything.

The export runs in the background and shows its progress. Stop ends it after the current recording; the table being written is discarded and the previous one is kept. Closing the window stops it too.

docs.title: Exporting again
docs.text:
Export into the same folder again and only new and changed recordings are read. The rows of every recording whose .mad has the same modification time as last time are copied from the existing tables, so an export of a run in progress mostly costs the recordings analysed since. A recording whose rows in the old table do not add up to the count in mad_recordings.csv is read again.

Nothing is copied when the settings differ from the last export (another harmonics setting, images turned on or off) or when the table format has changed. Turn Skip recordings unchanged off (--full on the command line) after updating FNT, so every value is computed with the current code.

Each table is written to a temporary file and swapped in only when complete, so a crash leaves the previous table as it was.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
# Recordings and detections of the most common model, every .mad under a folder
mad export --input /data/UltrasonicVocalizations_proc --out /data/usv_tables

# Which models analysed which recordings
mad export --input /data/UltrasonicVocalizations_proc --list-models

# A named model (or the unique start of its name), harmonics included
mad export --input /data/UltrasonicVocalizations_proc --out /data/usv_tables \
           --model 20261014_181834 --harmonics

# A project's labelled calls, with their images
mad export --project my_project/ --out /data/usv_tables --labels --images
Flag Meaning --input Folders (searched to the bottom) and/or wav files. --project The recordings registered in a MAD project (with or instead of --input). --out The output folder. --detections mad_recordings.csv and mad_detections.csv. The default when no table is named. --labels mad_labelled_calls.csv. --images mad_call_images/ (implies --labels). --model The model to export; default the most common. --list-models Print each model and its number of recordings, then stop. --harmonics Include harmonics. --full Read every .mad again instead of copying unchanged recordings. --settle-minutes Leave out .mad files written in the last N minutes (default 10).

It prints a line for each step and a progress line every 500 recordings.

docs.title: mad_recordings.csv
docs.text: Column Meaning path Full path of the recording. folder Name of the folder the recording is in. recording File name of the recording. channel Microphone channel from the file name (ch<N>…), when it has one. start Start time from the file name, yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:SS, when it matches Avisoft's ch<N><yyyy-mm-dd>_<HH-MM-SS>_<n>.wav; otherwise blank. This is the recorder's clock. duration_s Length of the analysed spectrogram, in seconds. model Model of the last inference (its run folder name). inferred_at When that inference ran. threshold Its probability threshold. detections Number of detections, harmonics included. calls Number of detections that are fundamentals (harmonic_n blank or 1). mad_mtime Modification time of the .mad, in seconds since 1970 (UTC). Used by the next export to tell what changed.

docs.title: mad_detections.csv
docs.text:
folder and recording join each row to its recording.

Column Meaning blob_id The detection's id in the .mad. start_s Onset, seconds from the start of the recording (the same time axis as the per-recording CSV). score The model's mean probability over the detection. status pending, accepted or rejected, from the review. harmonic_n, harmonic_call_id Harmonic grouping: 1 is the fundamental, 2 and up its harmonics; the call id groups them. Blank if grouping has not run. contour measures See below. ridge_turns, ridge_rate_hz, ridge_depth_khz, ridge_trill Brightness ridge (mad add-ridge): turns of the brightest continuous path through the mask, half the turns per second of call (Hz), median kHz between successive turns, and 1 for a trill (at least 4 turns at 20 Hz or faster). Blank where the .mad holds no ridge.

docs.title: mad_labelled_calls.csv
docs.text: Column Meaning path, folder, recording, channel As in mad_recordings.csv. rec_start The recording's start time from its file name (as start above). id The label's id in the .mad; also the image's file name. blob_id The detection it was accepted from; blank for a call painted by hand. painted TRUE for a call painted by hand. class Call class. start_s, stop_s Onset and offset, seconds from the start of the recording. min_freq_hz, max_freq_hz The call's frequency box. harmonic_n, harmonic_call_id, f0_hz Harmonic grouping. score, model_name Score and model of the detection it was accepted from. note, tags What the reviewer wrote on the call. peak_freq_hz … aspect_ratio MAD's call metrics, recomputed from the audio, as in the per-recording CSV (see the technical reference). contour measures See below. ridge_* The label's own brightness ridge. image, img_col0, img_col1, f_bin0, f_bin1 The image's file name, and where the call is in it, counted from 1: its first and last columns, and its lowest and highest frequency bins (bin 1 is 0 Hz). Blank without images. mad_mtime As in mad_recordings.csv.

docs.title: Contour measures
docs.text:
Measured from the call's own mask, without the audio. The contour is the mask's mean frequency in each time frame.

Column Meaning duration_ms Width of the mask. f_mean_khz Mean of the contour. f_min_khz, f_max_khz Lowest and highest frequency of the mask. f_start_khz, f_end_khz First and last value of the contour. slope_khz_ms (end − start) / duration. contour_sd_khz Standard deviation of the contour. turns Reversals of the contour by more than one frequency bin. max_jump_khz Largest frame-to-frame change of the contour. thickness_khz Mean height of the mask per time frame. area_px Pixels in the mask.

turns follows the mask's centre and counts small reversals; ridge_turns follows the brightest line inside the mask and counts excursions of at least 3 kHz. A blob-shaped mask over a fast trill has few turns and many ridge_turns.

docs.title: Mask Audio Detector (MAD)
docs.text:
MAD detects and classifies vocalizations using a custom deep-learning pipeline. Rather than hand-tuned DSP thresholds, users label call regions directly on the spectrogram — with the help of a Segment Anything Model — and train a segmentation model that learns to find and classify calls automatically.

Launch from the FNT main GUI Audio tab → Mask Audio Detector (MAD).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Spectrogram generation — raw audio is converted to a time–frequency spectrogram (short-time Fourier transform) at the recording's native sample rate (up to 250+ kHz).
  • Interactive labeling with SAM2 — the user clicks on a vocalization and a Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) proposes a pixel-level mask for that call, dramatically accelerating annotation compared to manual painting.
  • Manual refinement — brush and eraser tools correct SAM2 proposals. Labels follow a pending → confirmed / rejected workflow to keep training data clean.
  • Training-data storage — confirmed call masks are stored as rasterized examples in a shared HDF5 store, paired with the corresponding spectrogram patches.
  • Semantic segmentation model — labeled examples train a U-Net (ResNet18 encoder, via segmentation-models-pytorch) to perform pixel-level call detection on spectrograms.
  • Batch inference — the trained model runs across recordings, producing per-pixel prediction masks that are thresholded and converted to discrete call detections with time, frequency, duration, and class metadata.
  • Iterative refinement — predictions are reviewed in the GUI, where the user confirms or corrects them, feeding new examples back into the training set.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
MAD follows SLEAP's project model: a project points at recordings where they already live, the way a SLEAP project points at videos. The project folder holds those path references, the training-data store, and trained model checkpoints — never copies of your audio, which for 250 kHz recordings would run to hundreds of MB per file. Detections are saved in a .mad file next to each recording.

There is a single Audio list: every recording the project knows about. Anything you confirm in it trains the model — there is no separate training set to curate. Large production runs stay outside the list via the Folder inference target, so recordings you are not curating never join the training set.

A project is optional until you train. You can add wavs, label them, load a model from any trained project, run inference and review the results with no project open — labels and detections save beside the audio either way. Training needs a project, because the model and its example store have to live somewhere.

Because recordings are referenced rather than copied, a recording that moves is a soft state: the row is flagged, but training, the example store and every saved detection keep working, and File ▸ Locate Missing Recordings… repoints a whole moved tree from one file. File ▸ Pack Project is the escape hatch — it copies the audio in, making the project self-contained for archiving or sharing.

docs.title: Detection output
docs.text: Each recording's masks, detections and review status live in its <recording>_FNT.mad file beside the wav. File ▸ Export Annotations to CSV… turns that into a standalone <recording>_FNT_MAD_annotations.csv per recording — the same per-file profile SLEAP and DeepLabCut use for video. For analysis across a run, File ▸ Export… (or mad export) writes folder-wide tables instead: one row per recording, one per detection and one per labelled call, with optional spectrogram images of the labelled calls. See Exporting tables. There is no interchange export: third-party formats (Raven, Audacity) are upkeep the project does not carry. If a downstream tool is ever needed, compatibility gets built then.

docs.title: Consecutive-detection merging
docs.text: A long call can surface as several adjacent blobs — split across inference tile seams or broken by a brief sub-threshold dip. Optional consecutive merging stitches these back into one detection: blobs that are close enough in time (and, by default, overlap in frequency) are combined into a single call with a union bounding box and an area-weighted confidence. The frequency-overlap gate keeps calls that are adjacent in time but separated in frequency — such as a harmonic and its fundamental — distinct. Enable it via the CLI (--merge-consecutive) or the MADInferenceConfig.merge_consecutive flag.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
MAD's train / analyze / embeddings pipeline is also available headless as the mad console script, for scripting into batch and HPC workflows:

# Run a trained model over a folder (recursive), merging split calls
mad analyze --model weights.pt --input recordings/ --merge-consecutive

# Train a model from a MAD project directory
mad train --project my_project/ --epochs 30 --device cuda

# Export per-detection embeddings for clustering / similarity analysis
mad embeddings --model weights.pt --input recordings/ --out embeddings.npz

# Folder-wide tables of recordings and detections (see Exporting tables)
mad export --input recordings/ --out tables/

# Add stored spectrograms, then brightness ridges, to existing .mad files
mad add-specs --input recordings/
mad add-ridge --input recordings/ --model <project>/models/<run>

Run mad <command> --help for the full option list.

docs.title: Call embeddings
docs.text: The embeddings command extracts a fixed-length feature vector for each saved detection by pushing its spectrogram patch through the trained model's encoder and global-average-pooling the deepest feature map (512 dimensions for a ResNet18 encoder). The output .npz holds the embeddings alongside each call's source file, id, time bounds, and class — ready for clustering calls by similarity, surfacing novel call types, or comparing repertoires across animals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• FFmpeg — required for ADPCM and other non-PCM WAV formats. See Installation.
  • PyTorch — required for model training and inference; a CUDA-capable GPU is strongly recommended. See GPU Support.

docs.title: MAD Workflow — from a new project to a finished batch
docs.text:
This is the practical, step-by-step path. It says what to click and why, and where the traps are. For how the pieces work (storage layout, the CSV columns, the normalization rule, resume semantics) see the technical reference in fnt/usv/usv_detector/MAD_README.md.

The loop you are running, end to end:

label a few calls → train → run on your labeled files → accept/reject
       ↑                                                       │
       └──── add breadth, retrain ◄──── evaluate ◄─────────────┘
                                          │
                                   good enough? → batch run over everything

Most of the time goes into the loop, not the batch. The batch is the easy part once the model is right.

docs.title: 0. Before you start
docs.text:
Three checks, once per machine.

GPU. Open MAD and go to Help ▸ Check GPU / CUDA setup…. It should say GPU ready. If it says PyTorch is CPU-only, it prints the exact pip command for your driver — run it in the fnt env and restart. Do not skip this: on CPU, inference runs at roughly realtime, which makes a 3,000-file batch a matter of months rather than hours.

Acoustic settings. nperseg / noverlap / nfft and the dB range are fixed for the life of a project and its models. The defaults (512 / 384 / 1024, −100…−20 dB) are right for 250 kHz rodent USV recordings. Changing them later means re-labeling, so decide now.

Normalization. db_norm is fixed by default. per_file normalizes each recording to its own range and generalizes better across trials with different gain and noise floors — but a label saved under one rule cannot be used under the other, and training will refuse a mixed store. Decide before you label. Reasonable default: stay fixed, get labeling breadth first, revisit if cross-trial performance disappoints.

docs.title: 1. Create a project
docs.text:
File ▸ New Project… Pick a folder that will hold the project metadata, the example store and the model checkpoints. It will not hold your audio.

A project references recordings where they already live, the way a SLEAP project points at videos. That keeps projects small (kilobytes, not hundreds of GB) and means one source of truth per recording. If you ever need a self-contained copy — to archive it or hand it to someone — File ▸ Pack Project copies the audio in.

docs.title: 2. Add audio
docs.text:
Add Folder… or Add Files… in the Audio panel. Add Folder offers the whole subtree when there is one, which is what you want for a nested experiment / mic / day layout.

Everything in the list is labelable, and every confirmed call in the list trains the model. There is no separate training set to manage: if a recording is in the list, its labels train; take it out and they stop.

Do not add your whole production set here. Add the handful you intend to label. Large batches run through the Folder inference target in step 8, which never touches this list.

A ⚠ row means the audio has moved or its drive is not mounted. Nothing is broken — labels, the training store and saved detections are all fine, only preview needs the file. File ▸ Locate Missing Recordings… repoints one file and fixes every sibling that moved with it.

docs.title: 3. Label your first calls
docs.text:
Click a recording. Zoom with ↑/↓ or the wheel; pan with ←/→. A 0.3–0.5 s window is comfortable for USVs.

Three tools, one key each:

Key Tool Use it for M SAM Click a call, get a proposed mask. Right-click to add a negative point. This is the fast path. P Paint Brush over pixels by hand. Wheel resizes the brush. E Eraser Trim a proposal.

Enter confirms the pending mask and saves it as a training example. Esc / Clear discards it. U undoes the last one.

What to label — decide once, write it down, hold to it. The model learns the boundary you draw; an inconsistent boundary teaches it that the boundary is ambiguous, and you get unstable low-confidence predictions in exactly that regime. A defensible policy for counting vocalizations:

  • Label every fundamental you can reliably trace, including faint and distant ones. Skipping faint calls under-counts animals far from the mic.
  • Do not label harmonics. Harmonic visibility tracks amplitude and distance, so labeling them turns one vocalization into 1–N detections and makes the count partly a measure of proximity to the microphone. Your training tiles span the full frequency axis, so an unpainted harmonic sitting above a painted fundamental is actively taught as not a call.
  • Pick a concrete faint-call floor (e.g. "a contour I can follow across ≥3 columns") and keep it. The CSV records snr_db per call, so you can filter later; labeling low preserves that option, skipping does not.

Aim for breadth over depth: thirty calls from each of twenty recordings across your trials beats a thousand calls from three. Generalization, not capacity, is what limits a first model.

docs.title: 4. Train a first model
docs.text:
In Run Training, open Training settings if you want to change them — you usually don't for a first model. The defaults are sensible:

  • U-Net + resnet18 for a first model. Move to resnet34/50 or HRNet (crisp thin contours) once you have a few thousand labels.
  • Max epochs 100, patience 20 — early stopping keeps the best checkpoint.
  • Augmentation on. It is the biggest lever against overfitting a small set.
  • Device auto picks the GPU.

Click Run Training. The live graph opens in its own window. If Then run inference on is set to anything but Nothing, those recordings are analyzed automatically on the new weights when training finishes — using the detection settings (probability threshold, minimum blob size) from Run Inference, so set those first if you want something other than the defaults. The model lands in the Model dropdown, selected.

Read the split line in the log. Training holds out whole recordings for validation when it can (split_level: file), so the reported score means "works on a recording it never saw". With labels on only one recording it falls back to holding out calls (call) or tiles (tile), and says so — those numbers are optimistic. With very unbalanced per-file label counts the split can hold out most of your data; check n_val_tiles rather than trusting the score.

docs.title: 5. Run on your labeled files and review
docs.text:
In Run Inference, tick Audio list with All, then click Run Inference. (To predict as soon as training finishes instead, set Run Training's Then run inference on dropdown before you train.) Predictions appear as pending (colored per the legend under Labeling Tools; colors follow the color map so they stay visible).

Review with the keyboard:

Key Action A Accept — saves it as a training example R Reject — keeps a visible record, and stores it as a hard negative D Delete — removes every trace S Skip N / B Next / Back Ctrl+Z Undo (covers the example store too) G Gallery — a grid of the pending calls, click to mark, Apply

Reject is worth the keystroke. A rejection is exactly a false positive a human identified, and it is fed back to the model as a negative example. This is also how harmonic suppression gets taught under the policy in step 3: reject the harmonics the model finds, and it learns to stop.

Q runs the selected model on just the visible window — useful for spot checks without a full run.

The Min score slider hides pending calls below a confidence. It never hides accepted or rejected calls, and the count label always says how many are hidden. The completion prompt will not claim a file is done while the filter is hiding calls.

docs.title: 6. Iterate
docs.text:
Add a few recordings from a different trial, channel or time of day. Run the current model on them, correct it, retrain. Two or three rounds of this is normally where a model goes from "finds the obvious ones" to usable.

Where to spend labeling time: sort the Detections list by Score and work the middle — calls near the decision threshold are where a label changes the model most. Confidently right and confidently wrong calls teach it little.

docs.title: When the spectrogram can't decide: Fusion QC
docs.text:
A running wheel, a mouse chewing or scrabbling in bedding, and a faint call can look alike in a spectrogram. If the arena was filmed, Fusion QC (right end of the controls bar) shows what was happening at the microphone over the view (plus 1 s either side):

  • the camera that watched the microphone, synced to the playhead both ways — Play the audio and the frame keeps pace; drag the video's slider, or play it silently, and the playhead line moves on the spectrogram;
  • the mice that camera's Mask Tracker model finds, outlined (every few frames; colours tell mice apart within a frame, they are not identities);
  • the RFID reads and visit bouts at the microphone's zone, one row per mouse, under the video;
  • Layout ▸ Arena: every camera at once, laid out as the arena is, each zone camera labelled with the mice RFID places in it at that moment — calls carry between zones, so a call on one microphone can come from the next zone;
  • frames during the selected detection get a red border.

It needs a video_qc.json in the project folder: how to read each recording's trial, channel and start time (from its file name or the Avisoft log), which camera watched each channel, where each camera's files are and how to read their start times, and optionally the Mask Tracker model per camera, the RFID tables, the arena layout and per-trial clock offsets. The fields are documented at the top of fnt/usv/usv_detector/mad_video.py. Without the file the button stays off.

Clocks: each sensor kept its own clock, so check the time a camera burns into its frames against the one Fusion QC prints above it, and set offsets_s (video) and rfid.offsets_s per trial once you know them.

docs.title: 7. Evaluate before you scale
docs.text:
Evaluate Model… (next to Load Project Models) scores the model at call level — precision, recall, F1 across a sweep of thresholds, from one inference pass. Training reports pixel Dice on tiles, which cannot tell you how many real calls you will catch or how much junk you will reject.

Read it carefully:

  • Use recordings you have fully reviewed. An unreviewed prediction is not ground truth, so re-detecting one scores as a false positive. The dialog says when precision is understated for this reason and by how many calls.
  • Use recordings the model was not trained on, or the numbers flatter it.
  • The best-F1 threshold is highlighted; Use Selected Threshold copies it into the inference settings. Raise it when false positives cost you review time, lower it when missed calls matter more.

docs.title: 8. The batch run
docs.text:
Tick Folder, click Choose Folder…, point it at the production tree. It scans once (recursively) and streams paths to the worker; thousands of files never become thousands of list rows.

Settings that matter:

  • Threshold / Min blob pixels — from step 7.
  • Batch size 8, mixed precision on — measured optimum on a 4070 Ti-class GPU; larger batches do not help this model.
  • Re-detect from scratch off — a normal run keeps hand-labels and reviewed calls and only regenerates pending predictions.

Then Run Inference. Every finished file is logged immediately, so a crash or a deliberate stop loses nothing: run it again and it offers to resume, skipping files already analyzed by this model at these settings. Retrain, re-run the same folder, and it correctly analyzes everything again.

For an overnight run without the GUI:

mad analyze --model <project>/models/<run>/weights.pt --input <folder> --device cuda

It resumes the same way (--no-resume to force a redo).

Batch Run Summary (Ctrl+B) is the triage view: per-file detection counts, calls per minute, scan speed. Sort by detections, filter to files with calls or to failures, double-click a row to open it for review.

docs.title: 8b. Getting a picture out
docs.text:
Copy View, at the right of the controls bar under the spectrogram, puts the current view on the clipboard as an image — window, frequency range, colour map, boxes, masks and labels exactly as they stand — ready to paste into a slide, a document or a message. The dpi box beside it chooses the resolution: 150, 300 (the default, and the usual journal minimum) or 600. File > Save View as PNG… (Ctrl+Shift+S) writes the same image to a file.

The picture keeps the panel's own geometry and physical size, so raising the dpi makes it finer rather than bigger, and it is tagged with that dpi so Word and PowerPoint place it at the intended size instead of guessing. A very large window is capped at 40 megapixels — 600 dpi on a full-screen panel lands nearer 450 — and the status bar says so rather than quietly under-delivering.

What the resolution is and is not. The view is re-rendered, not screengrabbed, so axes, tick labels, detection boxes, mask outlines and contours are drawn at the output resolution. That part is real at every zoom and it is most of the benefit. The spectrogram raster behind them is bounded by the analysis:

View width What the extra pixels buy 0.3 s nothing — 590 STFT columns against a ~1300 px panel, already interpolated 1 s 1.4x 2 s 1.8x 5 s 2.3x

The crossover is around a 0.7 s window: below it the view holds fewer columns than the panel has pixels, so there is nothing to recover; above it there is, and the copy recovers it. Vertically there is never anything to recover — 513 frequency bins against a 700–1300 px pane is always upsampling.

docs.title: 9. What you get
docs.text:
A run records itself in <recording>_FNT.mad beside the wav — masks, detections, review status and harmonic assignments in one HDF5 file. That store is the record; nothing else is written during a run.

File ▸ Export Annotations to CSV… turns it into one standalone <recording>_FNT_MAD_annotations.csv per wav — the same per-file profile SLEAP and DLC use. Export when you are done reviewing, not before: the CSV is a snapshot, and re-exporting after more review simply overwrites it.

File ▸ Export… (or mad export) writes the whole run as a few tables in one folder instead: one row per recording, one per detection and one per labelled call, with optional spectrogram images of the labelled calls. Exporting again into the same folder reads only the recordings that changed, so it can be re-run while a batch is still going. See Exporting tables.

Every row is one call: onset/offset, frequency box and contour metrics (peak, bandwidth, slope, excursion, sinuosity), spectral shape (centroid, entropy, tonality), power and SNR, sequence metrics (inter-call interval, local call rate), the model score, and status (pending / accepted / rejected). Columns are documented in the technical reference.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• "GPU present, but PyTorch is CPU-only." Step 0. It is the single biggest factor in how long everything takes.
  • Training refuses to start: "more than one dB normalization rule." Labels were saved under both fixed and per_file. Pick one and re-label the minority; a saved patch cannot be re-normalized.
  • Validation score looks great but the model is poor on new files. Check split_level. If it is call or tile, the score was measured on recordings the model trained on. Label a second recording.
  • A file shows ⚠. Its audio moved. Training and detections are unaffected; use Locate Missing Recordings… to restore preview.
  • Resume skipped files it should have analyzed / analyzed files it should have skipped. Resume keys on model and threshold and min-blob and the merge options. Change any of them and prior results are correctly not reused.
  • Accept-All on a file with the score filter set only accepts the visible calls. That is intentional; the count label tells you how many are hidden.

docs.title: Audio / USV
docs.text:
Tools for processing, detecting, and classifying ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) and other audio signals. Supports high-sample-rate recordings (up to 250+ kHz) commonly used in rodent vocal communication research.

Launch any tool from the FNT main GUI Audio tab.

docs.title: Mask Audio Detector (MAD)
docs.text:
Project-based spectrogram labeling, training, and inference tool. See the MAD Overview for a full description of the pipeline.

  • Interactive spectrogram viewer — pan, zoom, and adjust frequency range across the full recording
  • Paint-based labeling — brush and SAM2-assisted tools to paint call masks directly on the spectrogram
  • Label workflow — pending → confirmed or rejected annotations
  • Training — train a U-Net segmentation model on labeled examples within the GUI
  • Inference — run trained models on new recordings; review and correct predictions
  • Project system — references recordings where they live; the project folder holds the training data and models
  • Output — a <recording>_FNT.mad file beside each wav (masks, detections, review status), exported to CSV on request

docs.title: Classic Audio Detector (CAD)
docs.text:
DSP-based detection and labeling tool.

  • Spectrogram-based detection using configurable DSP parameters (threshold, frequency band, minimum duration)
  • Manual labeling — review detections and assign class labels
  • Random Forest classifier — train and run classifiers on labeled call features
  • Harmonic linking — associate fundamental frequencies with their harmonics
  • Batch processing — run detection across folders of recordings

docs.title: Compress Audio Files
docs.text: Batch WAV compression for archival storage — convert to FLAC (lossless) or other formats with folder-based batch processing, preserving sample rate and bit depth.

docs.title: Trim Audio File
docs.text: Interactive audio trimming with spectrogram visualization, visual start/end selection, frequency filtering, and heterodyne playback for previewing ultrasonic content in the audible range.

docs.title: USV Heterodyne Processing
docs.text: Batch conversion of ultrasonic recordings to audible heterodyne signals — mixes the recording with a carrier frequency (default 40 kHz) to shift ultrasonic content into the audible range, with band-pass filtering to isolate the difference frequencies.

docs.title: Audio format support
docs.text: The module uses soundfile for standard WAV formats and falls back to FFmpeg for exotic encodings (e.g., ADPCM). FFmpeg must be installed and on PATH for full format support — see Installation.

docs.title: Imaging
docs.text:
Microscopy image viewing, processing, and quantification tools for Zeiss CZI files. Designed for fluorescence microscopy workflows in neuroscience (e.g., immunohistochemistry, reporter imaging).

Launch from the FNT main GUI Imaging tab.

docs.title: CZI Viewer
docs.text:
Multi-channel microscopy image viewer and processor:

  • Load CZI files — reads multi-channel, multi-scene Zeiss CZI images
  • False coloring — assign colors to channels (GFP green, Cy3 magenta, DAPI blue, custom)
  • Per-channel adjustments — brightness, contrast, gamma, sharpness, and min/max display range
  • Background subtraction — Rolling Ball or Gaussian methods with configurable radius
  • Channel merging — composite overlay of selected channels
  • Annotations — add text labels and shape annotations directly on the image
  • Export — save processed images to PNG or TIFF

docs.title: Image Quantification
docs.text:
Cell counting and analysis tool for CZI images:

  • Multi-channel detection — detect cells/particles per channel with configurable thresholds
  • Watershed separation — split touching cells using watershed segmentation
  • Colocalization analysis — measure co-expression across channels via centroid overlap and Dice coefficient
  • ROI-based density — draw regions of interest and calculate cell density (cells/mm²)
  • Export — results to CSV for downstream statistical analysis

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The Imaging tools need these optional packages:

pip install aicspylibczi fsspec Pillow scikit-image
  • aicspylibczi — reads Zeiss CZI file format
  • fsspec — required by aicspylibczi
  • Pillow — image export and annotation rendering
  • scikit-image — background subtraction (rolling ball) and watershed segmentation

docs.title: Mask Tracker
docs.text:
Label animals in video frames with SAM, train a YOLO instance-segmentation model on them, review its predictions, and run it over whole videos. One window does the labelling, training and review; a command-line tool does the long runs.

Launch from the FNT main GUI: Video tab ▸ FNT Tracking Tools ▸ Mask Tracker, or from a terminal in the fnt env:

python -m fnt.videoTracking.mask_tracker_gui --project <project folder>

The loop:

pick frames → label (SAM) → train → predict the unlabelled frames → accept / reject / fix
      ↑                                                                  │
      └──────────── frames where the model is weakest ◄──────────────────┘

docs.title: The project folder
docs.text:
A project lives next to the video it is for:

<project>/
    project_config.json        videos, classes, the ROI
    LABELING_GUIDE.md          the project's labelling rules (optional)
    training_frames/*.png      the frames you label
    annotations/annotations.json   labels, predictions, empty/skipped flags (COCO)
    models/<date>_<time>_<arch>_n=<frames>/   one folder per training run
    focus_*.txt                frame lists for --focus sessions

Labels save on every action; there is no Save step to forget. Two windows open on the same project do not see each other's changes: close one before working in the other, and reopen a window after a training run has written predictions.

docs.title: Labelling
docs.text:
The Training Frames Queue lists the frames to label. Frames come from the source videos (arrow keys scrub the video; E extracts the frame on screen to the queue) or from a script (mask_tracker_cli extract-frames, below). --focus <list.txt> opens the window on just those frames.

Key Does M SAM: click each animal; a click on or near a pending one adds to it, Shift+click starts a new one, right-click excludes a spot. Enter saves each as its own mask. P / X Paint / Eraser on a pending or saved mask (wheel = brush size) U, Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z Undo a click or stroke; undo / redo E Mark the frame empty: no animals (it trains as background) S Skip: leave the frame for now and go to the next one to label N / B Next / back in the queue Space / Shift+Space Next / previous queue frame along this video's timeline ← → (Shift ±10, Ctrl ±100) Scrub the source video; landing on a queue frame opens it with its masks V Show / hide the masks (and the ROI shading) 1–9, 0 Class: save the pending mask as that class, or switch the active class

The timeline under the frame marks the queue's frames from this video: green labelled, yellow predicted, white still to do.

Small animals. Zoom in (scroll) before you click: SAM sees what you see. Label every animal in a frame, or the model learns the ones you left as background.

docs.title: Labelling guide
docs.text: Guide (next to ROI) shows the project's rules on hover and opens them to read or edit. They are kept in LABELING_GUIDE.md in the project folder, travel with portable sessions, and MAD has the same button. Write a rule down the first time you make a judgement call (a mouse half in an entrance, a mouse seen through a lid) so every session, and every labeller, makes it the same way.

docs.title: Region of interest
docs.text:
A fixed camera sees more than the animals' space: the room around the arena, the lids of boxes the animals hide under. ROI draws, once per project, where the model may look:

  • Include area: click the corners of the area the animals can be in. The model sees only the box around it, so each animal has more pixels at the same input size; everything outside the outline is filled flat grey.
  • Exclude area: holes in that area the model must ignore (a lid it sees mice through).

Close an outline by clicking its first corner again (or double-click, right-click, Enter); drag a finished outline's corners to adjust it. Show what the model sees previews the prepared frame. The preview then shades what the model won't see (dark outside, red hatching in holes).

The ROI is saved in project_config.json and copied into each model trained after it is drawn. Training cuts frames and labels to it, and every way of running that model (post-training prediction, Predict, infer-videos, the behaviour tools, MAD's Fusion QC) prepares frames the same way, maps the masks back to full-frame coordinates and drops detections centred outside the area. Models trained before the ROI keep seeing whole frames.

Note

This is not FNT's separate ROI Tool (zones for occupancy analysis of finished tracks).

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Train Model (bottom of the Mask tab) trains on the approved frames: those with labelled masks or empty. Pending predictions and skipped frames are left out. The run opens a training window with the loss, validation mAP and live predictions on a few validation frames.

The same run from a terminal (useful for overnight runs):

python -m fnt.videoTracking.mask_tracker_gui --project <project> --focus <list.txt> \
    --train --training-window-only --arch yolo11n-seg --imgsz 1600 --batch 2 \
    --epochs 200 --patience 60 --augment --aug-rotation 180 --mosaic 1.0 \
    --copy-paste 0.5 --post-infer --post-infer-conf 0.25
  • --imgsz: input size. 640 is fine for large animals; small mice in a wide view want 1280-1600 (and an ROI). On a 3 GB card, 1600 needs --batch 2.
  • --augment --aug-rotation 180: flips, rotation, scale and brightness; 180 for top-down cameras, 15 for side views.
  • --copy-paste: animals pasted between training frames by their masks; strong with few labelled frames.
  • --post-infer: when training ends, the model predicts the queue's frames that have no approved mask, for review.
  • --train-only <list>: train on a subset of the frames.
  • --optimizer and --lr combine: picking an optimizer resets the learning rate to its default (SGD 0.01, AdamW 0.002) only when --lr is not given.

The run's model, plots and summary go in the project's models/ folder. The YOLO copy of the frames that training reads is built in a temporary folder on the local disk and removed when the run ends. On Windows, a mapped drive is opened by its network path (Z: becomes \\server\share), and without long-path support a label file 260 or more characters deep cannot be opened, so YOLO would train that frame as empty; the short local copy avoids that, and a run whose paths are still too long stops with an error instead.

docs.title: Reviewing predictions
docs.text:
Predictions appear yellow. A accepts the bold one (click another to pick it), R rejects it, Shift+A accepts all on the frame; a SAM click on a prediction replaces it with SAM's mask, and Paint / Eraser fix it before you accept. Next to Review jumps to the next frame with predictions. A rejected spot is not offered again on that frame. A frame whose every prediction you rejected, with nothing labelled, counts as empty (it trains as background); E unmarks it. The queue's Annotations column counts rejections as ✗.

--predict <model folder> (or File ▸ Predict Unreviewed Frames with a Model…) runs any trained model over the queue's unreviewed frames.

The same without the window, e.g. on the CPU while another job has the GPU:

python -m fnt.videoTracking.mask_tracker_cli predict-frames --project <project> \
    --model <model folder> --focus <list.txt> --device cpu

The next frames worth labelling are the ones the model gets wrong: low-scored masks, animals it missed, counts that jump. Pick them from videos and trials the model has not seen.

docs.title: Whole videos
docs.text:
python -m fnt.videoTracking.mask_tracker_cli infer-videos --model <model folder> \
    --videos <folders, files or a .txt list> --step 250

Segments every --step-th frame and writes <video>_masks.h5 beside each video (masks as RLE, scores, boxes, centroids). It resumes where it stopped and skips videos already done with the same model and settings; --order coarse (the default) spreads the work over every folder and camera first, so a stopped run is still an even sample.

behavior-window runs the model on every frame of a stretch of video and links the masks into tracks, with candidate behaviour bouts for review.

docs.title: Labelling on another machine
docs.text:
A focus list can be labelled anywhere FNT is installed, e.g. on a laptop through OneDrive:

python -m fnt.videoTracking.mask_tracker_cli pack-session --project <project> \
    --focus <list.txt> --out "<OneDrive>/sessions" --note "what to do"

copies the frames and their labels into a session folder that opens as an ordinary project (README.txt inside says how). When it's done:

python -m fnt.videoTracking.mask_tracker_cli unpack-session --session <session folder>

merges the labels back frame by frame (the project's annotations.json is backed up first). A frame whose labels changed in the project since packing stops the merge, unless --force; --dry-run reports without writing.

docs.title: RFID Tracking
docs.text:
Preprocessing for passive RFID (PIT-tag) tracking with Biomark readers: animals wear one or more tags, and antennas at resource zones record every pass. The tool turns the reader downloads into analysis-ready tables and tells you what it had to throw away and why.

Launch from the FNT main GUI RFID tab → RFID Preprocessing Tool.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Loads Biomark downloads ("Export All Records To File") as .xlsx, .xls, .txt (fixed-width) or .csv, from one or more folders. Overlapping downloads are deduplicated on scan time, reader, antenna and tag.
  • Guards against truncated exports. When a .txt and an .xlsx of the same download sit side by side, the spreadsheet is used and the .txt is checked against it; a .txt with fewer records, or one whose last line is cut mid-record, is reported. (In one real dataset 8 of 32 .txt exports stopped at ~61,000 rows while their .xlsx twins ran to 137,000.)
  • Reads the animal metadata from a spreadsheet as people keep it: header row detected (or chosen), columns mapped in a dialog, any number of tag columns, and Excel dates/times in whatever form they arrive.
  • Describes the arena as paddocks, readers, zones and antennas. Zones are named by paddock and zone (A1…A8, B1…B8) and antennas are keyed by (reader, antenna), so two paddocks whose readers both number their antennas 1–16 are kept apart. Several antennas per zone (e.g. an entrance "wall" antenna and a "floor" antenna) is normal; one per zone works too.
  • Cleans: unknown tags, unmapped antennas, reads by another paddock's reader (kept as flagged visits by default), optional release/trap windows, lost tags, and animals found dead.
  • Builds bouts and per-day summaries: zones entered, minimum distance, time in zones, zone holders, and pairwise co-occupancy.
  • Writes QC reports for everything above, shown as tabs in the window and saved as CSVs.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Reader Downloads → Add Folder… for each download folder. Folders are only ever read.
  2. Animals (metadata) → Choose File…, pick the sheet, then Columns… to check the header row and which columns hold name, sex, trial / home paddock, phase, code, tags, release and trap date/time.
  3. Arena → Edit Arena… → pick a preset (Liddell 8-zone paddock, Two Liddell 8-zone paddocks, One antenna per zone) and adjust. On the Paddocks tab, list each paddock's readers and the metadata trial values of the animals that live there. The antenna table can be imported from / exported to CSV (reader, antenna, zone, location, paddock, x, y).
  4. Time: timezone (for gaps across a DST change; leave blank if the reader clock never changes), and when day 1 starts (days run noon to noon by default).
  5. Check (no export) runs everything and fills the QC tabs without writing anything.
  6. Read the Two places and Stationary tags tabs. Right-click a row to mark a tag as lost from that day, or an animal as found dead; fine-tune under Animals & Tags….
  7. Run and Export.

docs.title: Cleaning rules
docs.text:
Rule What it does Why Unknown tags Reads of tags no animal wears are dropped and listed Test tags, strays Unmapped antennas Reads on a (reader, antenna) the arena does not describe are dropped and listed Usually an incomplete antenna table Other paddock's reader Keep (default, away = true), drop, or fold into the animal's own paddock (legacy) A hole in a shared wall makes these real visits Release / trap windows Optional: trim each animal to its metadata release and/or trap time, or to manual times Pre-release reader tests, post-trapping reads Lost tags A tag off its animal from a time (to a time): its reads inside are dropped A tag lying in a tube keeps being read and places the animal there Found dead Cut at the last entry (+ one bout gap), or at a manual time A body in a zone is read like a resident that never leaves

An entry is a read on an entrance-type antenna (location wall by default, configurable) after a gap longer than the bout gap. A mouse cannot help making entries; a body cannot make one. When the time a body was found is given, entries after it are ignored.

Tags are compared as 12-decimal strings, because spreadsheets store tag numbers as numbers and drop trailing zeros (985.11300454831 is tag 985.113004548310).

docs.title: Bouts and days
docs.text:
Per animal, consecutive reads in the same zone no more than the bout gap apart (default 50 s) form a bout; a zone change, a longer gap, or the day boundary ends it. A lone read is a 1 s bout. Days run from the day-1 origin to the same time the next day (noon to noon by default), numbered so that day 1 is (origin, origin + 24 h].

A legacy option reproduces the original R pipeline's bout rule for regenerating published numbers; it pairs bout starts and stops by position and occasionally joins reads across a zone change, so it is not the default.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Everything goes to <name>_FNT_analysis beside the download folders (never inside one), or a folder you choose:

<name>_FNT_analysis/
    fnt_config.json          every setting + provenance (FNT version, run time,
                             each input file's size and modification time)
    <name>_messageLog.txt
    csvs/
        <name>_reads.csv             animal, tag, reader, paddock, antenna, location,
                                     zone, zone_id, away, day, t
        <name>_bouts.csv             one row per bout
        <name>_animal_days.csv       reads, bouts, zones entered, minimum distance,
                                     time in zones, per animal and day
        <name>_zone_holders.csv      per paddock-zone-day: the male with > 50% of
                                     that zone's male reads, or 'contested'
        <name>_co_occupancy.csv      per day and pair: seconds in the same zone
                                     at the same time
        <name>_qc_*.csv              files, animals, unknown tags, unmapped antennas,
                                     cross-paddock visits, two places at once,
                                     stationary tags, found dead, dropped reads

Minimum distance is the sum of straight lines between the centres of consecutive distinct zones, within a paddock only (a move between paddocks adds nothing: the route is unknown). The holder share threshold and sex are configurable.

Reading the CSVs

Read the tag column as text. A tag number read as a float displays with fewer digits and can stop matching.

docs.title: QC reports
docs.text: Tab / file Look for Files Truncated .txt twins, malformed last lines, files skipped as "not a download" Animals Reads, days, first/last read against release/trap; animals never read; reads removed by each rule Unknown tags Tags read that no animal wears Cross-paddock Visits through a shared wall, per animal Two places Animal-days whose two tags each live mostly (> 80%) in different zones: a lost tag Stationary tags Tag-days read by one antenna in most hours: with no entries a body or a dropped tag; with entries on the one antenna, a tag lying at an entrance Found dead Last entry, cut time and reads removed per animal Dropped reads Reads removed by each rule

docs.title: Optional layers
docs.text: Group-by-individual matrix (GBI), co-presence edgelist, male displacement events, Hinde contact indices and social networks (needs python-igraph) are carried over from the earlier module. They run on the new zone IDs and are tested, but they are interpretive, so they are off by default (Bouts & Summaries → Optional layers).

docs.title: UWB Tracking
docs.text:
Preprocessing and analysis tools for Ultra-Wideband (UWB) positional tracking data. Designed for multi-animal tracking systems (e.g., Qorvo/Decawave DWM1001) used in field and laboratory neuroethology.

Launch from the FNT main GUI UWB tab.

docs.title: UWB PreProcessing Tool
docs.text:
Interactive GUI for loading, cleaning, and exporting UWB tracking data:

  • Load raw data from .db (SQLite) or .csv files containing timestamped tag positions
  • Tag identity mapping — assign animal IDs, sex, and metadata to each UWB tag
  • Deployment windows and off-animal intervals — a Start/Stop per tag, plus any number of intervals when a tag was reporting but not on its animal (e.g. a head cap found off and re-attached); fixes in either are dropped from the preview and every export
  • Coordinate smoothing with configurable Savitzky-Golay filter parameters
  • Timezone handling — convert UTC timestamps to local time
  • Day/night segmentation based on a configurable light cycle
  • Visual preview of smoothed trajectories per tag
  • Weather, sunlight and sky for the site (latitude/longitude you enter or load from a site profile): a weather line, a daylight strip, the moon's phase, and a sky icon (clear, partly cloudy, overcast, fog, light/moderate/heavy rain, snow, thunderstorm) that follows the playhead in the preview and the video. Measured data win: rain comes from the weather station's gauge wherever it has a record and daytime cloud from measured sunlight; the Open-Meteo model fills only gaps and what nothing measures (night cloud, thunder, fog), and is labelled "model". Exported minute by minute to {db}_sky.csv with the evidence behind each minute
  • Regions of interest — draw regions on the arena (or import the site XML's zones) for visit and occupancy tables
  • Contact and chases — contact bouts between every pair of animals within a distance threshold, and directed chase bouts
  • Export cleaned data, social and region tables, plots and animations, one trial at a time or as a batch queue

docs.title: Exports
docs.text:
Everything goes to <database>_FNT_analysis/ beside the database, with the settings in fnt_config.json. The tables are in csvs/:

File One row per <db>_smoothed.csv fix of a configured tag inside its deployment window: raw and smoothed positions (m), local time, animal <db>_raw.csv the same fixes before smoothing (optional) <db>_SocialOverlapBouts.csv contact bout of a pair: animal1, animal2, Day, Date, bout_start, bout_stop, duration_s, mean_distance, n_reads <db>_behavior_events.csv directed chase: behavior, actor, target, sexes, Day, bout_start, bout_stop, duration_s <db>_ROI_bout_occupancy.csv visit to a drawn region: SexID, Day, ROI, bout_start, bout_stop, duration_s, n_reads <db>_ROI_DailySummary.csv animal, region and day: time in the region and its rank among the animals that entered <db>_sky.csv minute: weather, daylight and sky state, with the evidence for each

Contact bouts are specific to the distance threshold and the bridging gap chosen at export; export again to try other values. Plots go to plots/ and tracking or social-network animations to animation_*/.

docs.title: Input data format
docs.text:
The tool expects UWB data with at minimum:

Column Description Timestamp ISO 8601 timestamp (UTC or local) shortid UWB tag identifier location_x X position (metres) location_y Y position (metres)

Additional columns (e.g., location_z, location_quality) are preserved during export.

Positions for analysis

Use smoothed_x and smoothed_y from <db>_smoothed.csv, at 1 Hz or finer. Tag read rates can differ several-fold between animals, so time spent anywhere is a sum of per-fix durations, never a count of fixes.

docs.title: Video Processing
docs.text:
Video preprocessing, editing, and behavioral annotation tools. All video operations use FFmpeg under the hood.

Launch any tool from the FNT main GUI Video tab.

docs.title: Video PreProcessing
docs.text:
Batch video preprocessing combining downsampling, re-encoding, and format conversion:

  • Resolution control — downsample to a target resolution
  • Re-encoding — convert between codecs (H.264, H.265, etc.)
  • Format conversion — change container format (.mp4, .avi, .mkv)
  • Quality presets — CRF-based quality control
  • Batch processing — process entire folders with progress tracking

docs.title: Video Trim and Crop
docs.text:
Interactive trimming and cropping with visual preview:

  • Scrubber-based navigation — preview any frame
  • Set start/stop times or specify a duration
  • Polygon crop regions — draw arbitrary crop shapes on the preview frame
  • Batch processing — configure settings for multiple videos, then process all at once

docs.title: Video Concatenation
docs.text: Join multiple video files within directories — automatic ordering by filename, FFmpeg concat demuxer for lossless joining of compatible streams, with progress tracking.

docs.title: Behavior Scoring Studio
docs.text:
Manual behavioral annotation tool for ethogram-based video scoring:

  • Define ethograms — custom behavior categories with color coding
  • Video playback with frame-accurate scrubbing and adjustable speed
  • Timeline visualization — view and edit annotations on a temporal timeline
  • Keyboard shortcuts for rapid scoring
  • Export annotations to CSV and JSON

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• FFmpeg must be installed and on PATH — see Installation.
  • Video playback and frame extraction use OpenCV, installed automatically with fnt.

docs.title: Video Tracking
docs.text:
Interactive animal tracking using Meta's Segment Anything Model (SAM) combined with classical computer vision. Designed for common behavioral paradigms such as the Open Field Test.

Launch from the FNT main GUI Video tab → Video Tracking.

docs.title: Why SAM?
docs.text:
Traditional background subtraction requires extensive per-environment parameter tuning (lighting, reflections, shadows, enrichment objects). SAM provides:

  • Zero-shot segmentation — works on any object without training
  • Interactive setup — click on the animal once, then tracking runs automatically
  • Robustness to clutter — handles reflections, shadows, and enrichment objects
  • Minimal per-video setup — suited to batch processing

docs.title: Tracking pipeline
docs.text:
1. User clicks on the animal → SAM segments it
  2. Optical flow tracking → fast frame-to-frame tracking (every frame)
  3. Periodic SAM updates → refine segmentation every N frames (default 30)
  4. Kalman filter → predict position during occlusions
  5. CSV export → trajectory plus behavioral metrics

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Select videos — one or more (supports batch processing)
  2. Select the SAM checkpoint — a downloaded .pth file; choose model type (vit_h/vit_l/vit_b) and device (cuda/cpu)
  3. Set up tracking — load the first frame, click on the animal, and draw the arena ROI
  4. Run tracking — watch the real-time trajectory visualization; cancel any time
  5. Outputs — {video}_trajectory.csv (frame-by-frame position) and {video}_oft_metrics.txt (behavioral summary)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Notes SAM update interval 30 frames Lower = more accurate but slower Confidence threshold 0.5 Below this, switches to Kalman prediction Model vit_h / vit_l / vit_b Accuracy vs. speed tradeoff

docs.title: SAM model checkpoints
docs.text:
Model Size Download ViT-H (Huge) 2.6 GB sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth ViT-L (Large) 1.3 GB sam_vit_l_0b3195.pth ViT-B (Base) 375 MB sam_vit_b_01ec64.pth

Use ViT-H for best accuracy, ViT-B for faster processing on limited hardware. GPU acceleration is strongly recommended — see Installation.
